Lipoplex Nanoparticle-Based RNA Delivery to 3D Melanoma Spheroids.
Lipoplex nanoparticle-based vaccination technologies have shown tremendous efficiency for in vivo transfection during the COVID-19 pandemic and also hold promise for treating melanoma. While pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics need careful in vivo and clinical testing, other parameters of drug performance can be assessed with in vitro systems as well. Spheroids composed of more than one cell type can serve to assess drug penetration, cell-type specificity, and transfection efficiency at an early stage of drug development.

Differentiating Avian and Seasonal Influenza Viruses in Wastewater by Digital PCR.
Highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5Nx) viruses, particularly clade 2.3.4.4b, pose substantial global health risks. We combined and piloted 2 duplex reverse transcription digital PCRs to discriminate between avian and seasonal influenza viruses in wastewater. This approach enabled rapid, strain-specific detection to reduce ambiguity in environmental surveillance for influenza viruses.

Adjusted Indirect Comparison Between Epcoritamab-R2 and Tafasitamab-R2 in Relapse/Refractory Follicular Lymphoma.
Treatment of relapsed refractory follicular lymphoma (R/R FL) still remains challenging. Several strategies have been used against R/R FL. Recently, two chemotherapy-free regimens have gained space, epcoritamab-lenalidomide-rituximab (Epco-R2) and tafasitamab-lenalidomide-rituximab (Tafa-R2). Herein, we performed an indirect trial comparison (ITC) between the two regimens using the Bucher method as they both have the common comparator arm R2. The ITC between the two study arms showed an overall response rate (ORR; p = 0.020), and complete remission rates (CR; p < 0.0001), in favor of Epco-R2. Analysis regarding time to next treatment (TTNT) interval also favored Epco-R2 (p = 0.0011). The ITC in the progression free survival (PFS) context showed the anchored comparison favored Epco-R2 over Tafa-R2 [HR 0.51 (95% CI 0.31-0.86)], p = 0.011, a finding more pronounced in patients with progression of disease within 24 months (POD24) negativity. Regarding the safety profile, Epco-R2 was associated with more hematological toxicity and infections, whereas, Tafa-R2 was associated with more COVID-19 infections probably reflecting the pandemic era enrollment timing. In conclusion, Epco-R2 is more effective in terms of treatment outcomes, but comes with greater toxicity. Tafa-R2 seems more suitable for patients with limited bone marrow reserves, patients who wish to avoid hospitalization, patients at a higher risk for cytokine release syndrome, and patients with high-risk infection vulnerability. Finally, this is not a direct comparison of two therapeutic regimens and the results should be cautiously interpreted. Treatment choice should be decided on a case-by-case scenario based on several different variables.

Phase-Specific Changes in Korean Adolescents' Health Behaviors and Mental Health Across COVID-19 School Closure and Reopening.
BACKGROUND: The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted school routines, but health changes during school reopening remain unclear. This study examined phase-specific changes in health behaviors and mental health among Korean adolescents. METHODS: Nationally representative Korea Youth Risk Behavior Survey data (2018-2024) were analyzed across pre-pandemic, pandemic, transition, and post-pandemic phases. Outcomes included health risk behaviors, diet and physical activity, obesity, and mental health indicators. Weighted prevalence estimates and logistic regression models were used. RESULTS: The analytic sample included 376,066 adolescents (51.8% boys). Current smoking declined from 6.4% (95% CI, 6.1-6.7) pre-pandemic to 3.8% (3.6-4.0) post-pandemic, whereas breakfast skipping increased from 34.5% (34.0-34.9) to 41.6% (41.1-42.0). Although moderate-to-vigorous physical activity exceeded its pre-pandemic level post-pandemic, obesity prevalence increased from 10.9% (10.7-11.2) to 12.2% (11.9-12.5). Suicidal ideation decreased during the pandemic but peaked at 14.0% (13.6-14.5) during transition. IMPLICATIONS FOR SCHOOL HEALTH POLICY, PRACTICE, AND EQUITY: During reopening, schools should strengthen healthy meal and physical activity programs, sustain substance-use prevention, and ensure equitable access to mental health screening and referral. CONCLUSIONS: Recovery was uneven across health domains, identifying school reopening as a critical prevention window requiring sustained, phase-specific intervention.

Mapping the Evidence for Oropouche Virus to Inform Research Prioritisation.
Oropouche virus (OROV) infection has gained increasing public health attention due to the ongoing outbreaks in South and Central America. The World Health Organisation (WHO) lists OROV as a priority pathogen for epidemic and pandemic preparedness. This work aimed to identify and categorise the available evidence on OROV to inform research prioritisation. We conducted a rapid mapping review (search date: up to 5 June 2025) to identify primary studies on OROV and categorised these by area of research, study design, and geographic region using a pre-defined framework. Included studies were displayed in an interactive evidence gap map (EGM) to identify any evidence gaps. In total, 269 primary studies on OROV were included and mapped into the EGM. Of these, the majority of data and findings were reported from South America, Central America and the Caribbean, reflecting the geographical epidemiology of OROV. The majority of studies were observational and descriptive, based on specific outbreaks. Limited evidence was found on vector surveillance, viral pathogenesis, diagnostics and immune correlates of protection. No experimental studies on potential therapeutics or vaccines conducted in humans were identified. The findings from our mapping review and EGM highlight the utility of this methodology to rapidly identify gaps in scientific evidence for emerging or re-emerging pathogens with outbreak potential. The EGM can be used solely, or in conjunction with other prioritisation tools, in order to focus investment and research efforts towards priority topics.

Risk Assessment of an Illegal Laboratory in Reedley, California, Using Geospatial Analysis of Open-Source Epidemic Intelligence Data.
An illegal laboratory discovered in Reedley, California, in December 2022 was in a warehouse, operating without a license, handling about a thousand transgenic mice, chemicals, and possibly over 20 pathogens, including vials labeled Ebola, which were never tested but destroyed. This study aimed to estimate epidemic signals around the Reedley illegal laboratory using open-source epidemic intelligence data. We utilized data from EPIWATCH, from October 2021 to October 2023, a year prior to and a year after the establishment of the illegal laboratory. The spatial pattern of outbreak signals was analyzed using hotspot analysis, and the distances of outbreak signals from the laboratory were measured. In California, an upward trend in outbreak signals of pathogens associated with the laboratory was noted in December 2022, April 2023, and August 2023. In the hotspot analysis, California and eight other states in the United States (US) were identified as hotspots. Narrative evidence revealed the presence of a sick employee working in the laboratory, whose child also became ill. Changes in disease patterns reported in California or the US in the year following the establishment of the illegal laboratory may or may not be linked to the illegal laboratory. A subsequent illegal lab linked to Reedley was identified in Las Vegas in 2026, highlighting the ongoing threat to biosecurity. EPIWATCH geospatial and temporal analysis can enhance the public health risk assessment of threats associated with illegal laboratories, especially when there is no available testing or reporting.

Respiratory pathogens across rural populations: general practice patients with community-acquired pneumonia, residents, and goat farmers.
BACKGROUND: Residents living near goat farms (< 2000 m) in the Netherlands have consistently shown an elevated risk of pneumonia, yet the pathogens underlying this association remain unknown. This study assessed the presence of 33 respiratory pathogens, including bacteria, viruses, and fungi, across rural populations with different goat farm exposures. METHODS: This cross-sectional study included general practitioner (GP)-diagnosed pneumonia patients (PP; n = 108), non-farming rural residents without pneumonia (NFR; n = 200), and goat farm workers (GFW; n = 91). Oropharyngeal and nasopharyngeal swabs were collected and analyzed by a multiplex and two additional PCR test targeting in total 12 bacteria, 20 viruses and 1 fungus. Between-group differences in detection were assessed by Fisher's exact tests. Logistic regression analyses were performed to assess associations between pathogen detection and residential proximity to goat farming and other covariates. RESULTS: Presence of any of the examined pathogens was highest in the PP group (94.5%), followed by GFW (88.8%), and NFR (70%). The most frequently detected pathogens overall were Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Moraxella catarrhalis, and rhinovirus. Of these, M. catarrhalis and S. pneumoniae were significantly more often detected in PP, whereas Salmonella spp. and S. aureus were more frequently detected in GFW. Eight pathogens, including Coxiella burnetii, were not detected. Age, season of sampling, smoking and other covariates were significantly associated with certain bacteria and viruses. However, no associations were identified between residential proximity to goat farming and detection of specific pathogens in NFR and PP. CONCLUSIONS: Respiratory pathogens were detected in nearly all PP, while substantial proportions of positives were also observed in GFW and NFR, likely reflecting (transient) colonization rather than active infection. Detection of the examined pathogens was not associated with residential proximity to goat farms, suggesting that these pathogens do not explain the observed increased pneumonia risk among nearby non-farming residents. As a substantial proportion of the Dutch population (~ 7%) lives within 2,000 m of a commercial goat farm, and goat farming is expanding globally, further research efforts, including microbiologic diagnostics and surveillance, are needed to elucidate the mechanisms underlying the increased pneumonia risk among nearby residents.

Spatiotemporal Trends in Suicide: Sociodemographic, Economic, and Environmental Factors.
Suicide is one of the world's leading public health problems, with more than 720,000 deaths annually. Suicide has traditionally been studied from an individual perspective. However, research has increasingly highlighted the influence of community-level factors on suicide risk. This study aimed to (1) analyze the spatial distribution of suicide mortality at the provincial level in Spain (2018-2022); (2) perform stratified analyses by sex and age group; and (3) compare suicide risk across different phases of the COVID-19 pandemic. We used data from the Spanish National Institute of Statistics on 17,809 suicide deaths in 47 peninsular provinces between 2018 and 2022. Covariates included sociodemographic (e.g., aging rate, population density), economic (e.g., unemployment, GDP), and environmental (e.g., temperature) indicators. Bayesian hierarchical spatial Poisson regression models were fitted to estimate suicide risk and identify relevant contextual variables. The general spatial model revealed a higher risk of suicide in provinces with lower population density, higher aging rates, and lower health expenditure. Other covariates such as gross domestic product, unemployment, or temperature were associated with specific sex or age groups. Suicide risk was highest in the northwestern provinces and lowest in the central regions. Stratified analyses showed similar patterns across gender and age groups, and between time periods, with some variations in spatial distribution. This study reveals significant spatial heterogeneity in suicide risk across Spanish regions, influenced by sociodemographic, economic, and environmental factors. These findings underline the importance of regionally tailored suicide prevention policies, especially in aging and low-density areas with low health investment.

Specialty-stratified trends in oral cancer resection in Japan before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic: A National Database analysis (2016-2023) with comparative context from Germany.
In Japan, oral cancer resection is reimbursed under two parallel schedules: the medical K-code, claimed predominantly by otolaryngology/head-and-neck surgery (OHNS), and the dental J-code, claimed by oral and maxillofacial surgery (OMS). Specialty-stratified nationwide trends across the COVID-19 pandemic have not been described. Annual counts for 14 procedure categories in fiscal years 2016-2023 were extracted from the National Database Open Data of Japan and grouped by subsite and extent of resection. Three a priori periods were defined: pre-pandemic (2016-2019), pandemic (2020-2021), and post-pandemic (2022-2023). In total, 72 135 resections were captured (mean 9017/year), with OMS performing 53-58%. Volume decreased by 12.8% between 2019 and 2021, attributable almost entirely to OMS, and rebounded fully by 2023. OMS performed the majority of partial glossectomies (57%), marginal mandibulectomies (81%), and partial maxillectomies (66%), whereas OHNS performed most subtotal and en bloc procedures. The within-specialty partial-to-subtotal glossectomy ratio averaged 28 for OMS versus 3.5 for OHNS, consistent with an earlier-stage tongue cancer caseload. Paired K-code and J-code point values were identical and increased synchronously at every revision. No post-pandemic shift toward more extensive resection was observed, which was broadly consistent with the German experience, although these procedure counts lacked individual-level staging and cannot be used to assess stage migration directly.

COVID 19 and fungal infection - A double disaster:a case series.
The recent Coronavirus pandemic in 2019 [COVID-19] was associated with an increased risk of opportunistic fungal co-infection. This case series presents 5 autopsy-confirmed fungal co-infections identified in patients who died following COVID-19. Among the notable findings were Fusarium-associated fungal myocarditis and human infection with Hormographiella, an extremely rare pathogen found in COVID-19. To the best of our knowledge, the latter represents the first reported fungal co-infection with this pathogen in COVID-19. We also report the first postmortem diagnosis of invasive pulmonary mucormycosis in COVID-19 in Sri Lanka, confirmed with culture as Rhizopus spp. Postmortem examination, histopathological analysis and fungal culture revealed fungal infections that had not been suspected clinically or had been only partially characterized, and provided the microbiological and pathological evidence necessary for establishing the cause of death These findings highlight the medicolegal importance of thorough autopsy examination in severe COVID-19, especially in situations where opportunistic fungal infection may have contributed to death.

Aerobic physical activity is associated with lower pneumonia and COVID-19 mortality in adults with cognitive impairment.
Cardiovascular disease and pneumonia are major causes of death in dementia, but cause-specific mortality has rarely been examined in clinically confirmed cognitive-impairment cohorts. In this nationwide retrospective cohort study, 116,563 individuals with clinically confirmed mild cognitive impairment or dementia in the Korean Dementia Relief Center registry (2016-2021) were linked to health screening and death registry data. Aerobic physical activity (APA) was quantified in metabolic-equivalent minutes per week (MET·min/week). Cox proportional hazards and Fine-Gray models estimated adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) and subdistribution HRs (sHRs). The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure controlled the false discovery rate (FDR) across 18 cause-specific comparisons. During 400,500 person-years of follow-up (mean, 3.4 years), 5022 participants (4.31%) died. Compared with inactivity, low, moderate, and high APA were associated with lower all-cause mortality (HR [95% CI], 0.728 [0.652-0.813], 0.704 [0.636-0.781], and 0.636 [0.590-0.687], respectively). High APA was associated with lower pneumonia mortality (sHR, 0.554; 95% CI, 0.437-0.702) and COVID-19 mortality (sHR, 0.520; 0.368-0.735). These point estimates were numerically lower than for ischemic heart disease and cerebrovascular disease (sHRs, 0.613 and 0.630). Pneumonia mortality was lower across all APA levels after FDR control (q ≤ 0.023). The E-value for the high APA-pneumonia association was 3.01. APA was associated with lower mortality even at modest activity levels, especially for pneumonia deaths. Achievable activity goals may therefore merit prospective evaluation as part of supportive care for adults with cognitive impairment. Because APA may also indicate preserved physiological reserve, these findings do not establish causality and require confirmation using repeated, objective activity measurements.

Hospital-based surveillance of vaccine-preventable diseases in children: a retrospective study in a Dutch tertiary hospital (2024-2025).
BACKGROUND: Vaccine-preventable diseases (VPDs) are a major cause of morbidity in children, despite established immunization programs. Surveillance of VPDs is essential to inform public health strategies and strengthen national immunization programs. This pilot study evaluated the feasibility of using routinely collected hospital data for in-hospital surveillance of pediatric VPDs. METHODS: We performed a retrospective cohort study at a tertiary hospital in the Netherlands from July 2024 to June 2025, before national implementation of RSV immunization. Children <18 years admitted with laboratory-confirmed infections caused by pathogens with available licensed vaccines were included, regardless of inclusion in the national immunization program. Feasibility was assessed based on case ascertainment, completeness of key variables and availability of vaccination information. RESULTS: We included 99 children (103 VPD episodes; median age 0.6 years), of whom 60% (n = 59) required pediatric intensive care. Most hospitalizations were caused by respiratory infections, particularly RSV (n = 52) and influenza (n = 27). Case ascertainment required integration of multiple data sources, as 45% of children were tested outside the study hospital. Clinical variables were largely complete and vaccination status could be determined for 84% of episodes. Overall, 9% (n = 9) of VPD episodes occurred in fully vaccinated children. Most VPD episodes (76%; n = 78) occurred in children not vaccinated against the specific pathogen, mainly because they were too young or because the pathogen or serotype was not covered by the national immunization program or current guidelines. CONCLUSIONS: Retrospective hospital-based surveillance of pediatric VPDs is feasible and provides key information to guide efforts to optimize the national immunization program. By capturing disease severity and vaccine preventability, it complements existing surveillance data in the Netherlands.

Early Invasive Aspergillosis after Liver Transplantation: A Matched Case-Control Analysis of Clinical Features and Risk Factors in a Chinese Cohort.
BACKGROUND: Early invasive aspergillosis (IA) is a severe complication of liver transplantation, but data from Chinese recipients remain limited. We evaluated its clinical characteristics, outcomes, and independent predictors. METHODS: We retrospectively studied adult liver transplant recipients at the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang University from August 2018 to March 2023. Patients meeting 2020 EORTC/MSGERC criteria for proven or probable IA within 1 month post-transplant were matched 1:2 to non-IA controls by age, sex, and etiology. Postoperative ICU and intubation durations were excluded from multivariable regression to eliminate temporal bias. RESULTS: Among 1,051 recipients, 78 developed early IA (7.4% incidence; 3 proven, 75 probable), matched to 156 controls. Aspergillus fumigatus predominated (64.1%), with a median onset of 5 days. IA was associated with reduced 12-month survival (65.4% vs 80.1%, P = 0.014). Higher acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) grade, preoperative corticosteroid exposure, and postoperative 12-hour lactate >5 mmol/L were independent risk factors. CONCLUSIONS: ACLF severity, pretransplant corticosteroids, and early postoperative hyperlactatemia independently correlate with early IA. These hypothesis-generating findings help identify high-risk recipients requiring targeted surveillance.

Leishmania infection in dogs in Israel - A cross-sectional study.
Leishmania spp. are kinetoplastid protozoa that cause zoonotic disease in humans and animals. No large-scale cross-sectional survey has been performed to study canine leishmaniasis and its spatial distribution in Israel. We aimed to survey the prevalence and geographical distribution of Leishmania infection in dogs in Israel. Paired blood and sera were collected from domestic dogs at private clinics and animal shelters throughout Israel. Leishmania infection was determined by ELISA serology and blood qPCR targeting the kinetoplast minicircle (kDNA) and the ribosomal ITS1 region. Altogether, 1,392 paired samples were tested from dogs from all parts of Israel. Thirty nine of 1,392 (2.8%) dogs were seropositive to Leishmania. Leishmania spp. infection was detected in 35/1392 (2.5%) and 10/1392 (0.7%) dogs by kDNA and ITS1 qPCR, respectively. All ITS1 PCR-positive dogs were confirmed to be infected by Leishmania infantum after DNA sequencing. Seventy four of 1,392 (5.3 %) dogs were either seropositive or PCR-positive. ITS1 PCR-positive dogs were 20 times more likely to be seropositive than negative dogs (p < 0.001) while kDNA PCR-positive dogs were 5.1 times more likely (p = 0.003). Dogs with clinical signs suggestive of leishmaniasis had significantly higher prevalence of seropositivity (7.5%) compared to dogs without signs (2.2%; p= 0.001). This survey of Leishmania infection in dogs covering the entire region of Israel revealed widespread infection in the northern, central and mid-southern regions of Israel with dominance of sub-clinical infection. The risk of Leishmania infection warrants protection against vector sand fly bites and disease screening among dogs throughout Israel.

Biochemistry of protozoan Metacaspases: Structure, processing, and inhibition.
Metacaspases are calcium-dependent cysteine proteases (clan CD, family C14) present in fungi, protozoa, and plants but absent from mammals. Although structurally related to metazoan caspases, they differ in substrate specificity (cleaving after arginine or lysine), calcium-dependent activation, and monomeric architecture. In protozoan parasites such as Trypanosoma brucei, T. cruzi, Leishmania spp., Plasmodium spp., and Toxoplasma gondii, metacaspases regulate programmed cell death, cell cycle progression, protein quality control, differentiation, and virulence. Their absence in humans and essentiality in multiple parasitic life stages make them attractive drug targets for neglected tropical diseases. This review integrates structural, biochemical, functional, and pharmacological data on protozoan metacaspases. We examine calcium-dependent activation, the role of calcium homeostasis, functional diversification across parasite lineages, and the involvement of metacaspases in apoptotic and non-apoptotic pathways. Recent advances in small-molecule inhibitor discovery are covered, including oxime-based compounds, chalcones, flavonoids, peptidomimetics, and non-peptidyl scaffolds from virtual screening and rational design. A comparative biochemical analysis highlights species-specific differences in calcium dependence, processing, and regulation. Inhibitors are systematically classified by kinetic mechanism, offering a framework for understanding their mode of action and guiding structure-based drug design. We address selectivity challenges arising from metacaspase conservation across eukaryotes, distinguish experimentally validated binding sites from computationally predicted ones, and critically evaluate current in vivo and in vitro evidence for inhibitors in disease models. Finally, we discuss isoform redundancy, species-specific regulation, and translational development challenges, along with future research directions. Persistent Non-Falciparum Malaria in Kenya: Evidence from 17 Years of Sentinel Surveillance.
BACKGROUND: Human malaria is caused by several Plasmodium species, including P. falciparum, P. malariae, P. ovalecurtisi, P. ovalewallikeri, P. vivax, and P. knowlesi. Pf is the most virulent and the primary target of most interventions, although mixed-species infections are common. Non-falciparum species are more difficult to diagnose, treat, control, and eliminate. This study aimed to determine the burden of Plasmodium species among symptomatic individuals in selected regions of Kenya. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Between 2008 and 2025, a total of 4,255 blood samples were collected from symptomatic individuals presenting at healthcare facilities across 7 sentinel sites, namely, Busia, Kericho, Kisii, Kisumu, Kombewa, Malindi, and Marigat, and were analyzed for species composition via qPCR. RESULTS: Plasmodium falciparum was dominant in 4,139/4,255 (97.3% 95% CI 0.96-0.97), followed by P. ovalewallikeri 545/4,255 (12.8% 95% CI 0.11-0.13), P. malariae 235/4,255 (5.5% 95% CI 0.04-0.06), and P. ovalecurtisi 217/4,255 (5.1% 95% CI 0.04-0.05). Up to 3,460/4,255 (81.3%) were single-species infections. Between 2008 and 2025, P. falciparum remained the dominant species across all study sites, while mixed infections involving Plasmodium malariae, Plasmodium ovalecurtisi, and Plasmodium ovalewallikeri occurred intermittently at varying frequencies, indicating sustained transmission of non-falciparum species. The geographic distribution of Plasmodium single-species and mixed-species varied significantly across surveillance sites (x2 P = .000) with the Lake endemic region showing the greatest species diversity. CONCLUSIONS: Although Plasmodium falciparum remained the predominant species among symptomatic individuals, non-falciparum parasites, including Plasmodium malariae, Plasmodium ovalecurtisi, and Plasmodium ovalewallikeri, were consistently detected. The occurrence of mixed infections indicates persistent but low-level transmission of these species. These findings underscore the importance of sensitive multi-species diagnostic and surveillance approaches to better inform malaria control and elimination strategies.

Newcastle disease virus research: pioneering scientists, landmark discoveries, and virological innovations.
Newcastle disease (ND) has been recognized for a century as one of the most consequential viral diseases of poultry, and its scientific history provides a distinctive example of how sustained investigation of a single pathogen can drive advances across veterinary medicine, virology, immunology, epidemiology, molecular biology, vaccinology, and biotechnology. The severe outbreaks reported in Java, Indonesia, and Newcastle-upon-Tyne, England, during 1926 marked the beginning of the recognized scientific history of ND and initiated an international research effort that progressed from disease recognition and experimental characterization to diagnostics, vaccination, molecular pathogenesis, and genomic epidemiology. During the 1940s and 1950s, investigations of viral propagation, antigenicity, pathogenicity, and attenuation established the foundations of live and inactivated vaccination. From the 1960s onward, molecular investigations progressively elucidated the determinants of ND virus (NDV) replication, protein processing, and virulence, particularly the role of the fusion-protein cleavage site. The emergence of nucleotide sequencing and phylogenetic analysis during the 1980s and 1990s subsequently transformed strain characterization and provided the foundations for molecular epidemiology and genotype classification. Complete-genome sequencing and the establishment of reverse-genetics systems in the late 1990s further transformed NDV from an organism studied primarily through observation and isolation into a genetically tractable experimental system. Subsequent international efforts standardized NDV genotype nomenclature and enabled increasingly detailed analyses of viral evolution and geographic dissemination. In parallel, NDV research expanded beyond conventional disease control into recombinant vaccine development, systems-level host-virus studies, molecular diagnostics, and oncolytic virotherapy. This historical perspective traces these major scientific transitions from 1926 to 2026, emphasizing the investigators, experimental systems, conceptual advances, and technological innovations that collectively transformed NDV research from disease recognition into a multidisciplinary molecular and translational fields.

Co-circulation of H5N1 and H5N6 high pathogenicity avian influenza viruses in migratory birds at a coastal wintering site in China.
Since 2020, H5Nx high pathogenicity avian influenza viruses (HPAIVs) belonging to hemagglutinin (HA) clade 2.3.4.4b have undergone widespread dispersal in wild birds, posing substantial threats to global poultry populations and mammals worldwide. In this study, we report the co-circulation of clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 and H5N6 HPAIVs associated with mortality events in Anseriformes and Charadriiformes at a coastal wintering site in Fujian Province, China. H5N1 and H5N6 viruses were identified in four species of waterfowl (Bean Goose, Eastern Spot-billed Duck, Eurasian Wigeon, and Eurasian Curlew). Phylogenetic analysis indicated that these H5N1 and H5N6 isolates were clade 2.3.4.4b strains circulating within Eurasia and lacked known mammalian adaptation markers in key proteins. The infected birds exhibited severe systemic multi-organ pathology, with the most pronounced damage observed in the lungs. H5N6 and H5N1 viruses caused lethal injury in BALB/c mice, with H5N1 leading to systemic infection. Environmental sampling also revealed the presence of H5N1 HPAIVs alongside low-pathogenicity avian influenza viruses (LPAIVs) such as H3N1 and H6N1. Our findings highlight the complex and dynamic transmission patterns of H5 HPAIV in wild bird populations and the substantial threat they pose to mammals, underscoring the critical importance of sustained surveillance for high pathogenicity avian influenza in wild birds.

"Stuck in this loop": A qualitative study examining the impact of housing services bureaucracy interactions on people experiencing homelessness who use drugs.
The population of people experiencing homelessness (PEH) across the United States continues to grow as affordable housing stock for low-income renters becomes less available and government-led efforts to increase housing stock and provide subsidized housing lag. A range of community, non-profit, and government organizations have responded to this growth in the population of PEH, alongside the ongoing drug overdose crisis, using a range of both paternalistic and punitive approaches. These state-controlled, as well as public and private non-profit, social services bureaucracies involved in poverty governance have become increasingly hard to navigate and less capable of providing rapid, high-quality aid. This study examines the impact of interactions with this system on PEH who use drugs in Los Angeles County (LAC). Ethnographic participant observation was conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic, between February 2021 and March 2023, at four encampments of PEH in LAC. Semi-structured interviews with 30 PEH who use drugs were also conducted from October 2022 to March 2023. Interviewees described deeply strained interactions with housing and case management social services agents, agencies, and related non-profits that provide these services. They indicated consistent frustration at seeming bureaucratic unpredictability, conflicting and inflexible scheduling, and perceived mistreatment and blame for their situations. The cumulative effect of these interactions on participants and those observed was to diminish feelings of ontological security-defined as social and material constancy, stability of routines, and trust in one's environment-leaving them feeling stuck and with limited agency over their housing trajectories. These outcomes-frustration, mistreatment, and psychological and material insecurity-are situated within a services environment rife with underfunding, employee burnout and turnover, and state failure to adequately resource and monitor agencies. Our results indicate that structural changes to service provision are necessary to reduce worker turnover, provide social stability, and provide autonomy, respect, and flexibility to PEH who use drugs to strengthen ontological security and prevent further harm.

Improving equity in respiratory disease outcomes in Africa using data-driven tools: National Institute of Health Care and Research's (NIHR) EQUI-RESP-AFRICA project.
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, pneumonia, influenza, asthma, tuberculosis, lung cancer, and COVID-19 are all prevalent in Africa, where they cause a very large burden on the population's health, but are managed by health systems with a limited capacity for prevention, diagnosis, and treatment. They are also underlaid by substantial inequities in outcomes, with the poorest who have no access to care being affected the most. An interdisciplinary group of academics, policymakers, representatives of non-governmental organisations (NGOs), patients, and civil society are implementing a programme to address key respiratory diseases (RD) in five African countries where morbidity and mortality from RD is very large: Nigeria, Kenya, Cameroon, Cote d'Ivoire, and South Africa. The aim is to build capacity, conduct quality research and an intervention trial, and engage communities and policymakers in order to achieve demonstrable and equitable reductions in morbidity and mortality from RD through evidence-based improvements in prevention, diagnosis, treatment, interventions, and policies. The EQUI-RESP-AFRICA project will map the landscape of respiratory medicine in partner countries through rapid reviews of the available literature and data; engage relevant in-country stakeholders; study patients' and providers' preferences and needs; identify research priorities using the Child Health and Nutrition Research Initiative method; and conduct summer schools for capacity building in data science and machine learning/artificial intelligence, in community engagement, and in advocacy for and the use of the Equitable Impact Sensitive Tool (EQUIST) and Pathways to Survival (PATHS) tool. The project will also assess national health system preparedness for emerging infections, identify bottlenecks for early response, assess oxygen capacity and security, study adherence to international guidelines, and conduct qualitative studies to understand barriers to seeking care. It will also explore the feasibility of delivering a pulmonary rehabilitation programme through a randomised controlled trial. Ultimately, the programme will link evidence with policy using the EQUIST and PATHS tools to improve equity in outcomes and identify bottlenecks that lead to morbidity and mortality from respiratory causes. Through high-level meetings, it will prioritise the implementation of equitable interventions that are appropriate to each African context and tailored to patients' needs. A team of social scientists and NGOs, joined by a team of researchers of diverse backgrounds, will engage communities, stakeholders and policymakers to build capacity through summer schools, and disseminate the results through a dedicated project website, the Journal of Global Health, the Journal of the Pan-African Thoracic Society, collaborating NGOs, and mainstream and social media.

Cyclosporine treatment of ARDS due to severe COVID-19: The I-SPY COVID Adaptive Platform Trial.
RATIONALE: Aberrant host response to SARS-CoV-2 infection causes severe lung injury and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) with resultant multiorgan failure and death. Cyclosporine, a calcineurin inhibitor with potent immunosuppressant and direct antiviral properties, was hypothesized to reduce cytokine-driven injury in hospitalized patients with severe COVID-19 ARDS. OBJECTIVES: To evaluate whether cyclosporine improves time to recovery and reduces mortality in critically ill patients with COVID-19, using the I-SPY COVID adaptive platform trial design. METHODS: In this phase 2, multicenter, open-label, randomized controlled trial, non-intubated and intubated adults with confirmed COVID-19 requiring ≥6L/min oxygen received oral cyclosporine 5mg/kg/day in two divided doses for 5 days, added to standard backbone therapy (dexamethasone and remdesivir), or standard therapy alone. Co-primary endpoints were time to recovery and time to death, assessed using Bayesian proportional-hazard models with pre-specified graduation thresholds. RESULTS: Of 238 randomized patients (110 cyclosporine, 128 control), 28-day recovery rates were 65.9% vs. 71.1% and 28-day mortality rates were 10.7% vs. 11.3%, respectively. The posterior probability that cyclosporine improved recovery was 6% (graduation threshold >97.5%) and that it reduced mortality was 59.6% (graduation threshold >90%), meeting neither pre-specified efficacy criterion. Serious adverse events were more frequent with cyclosporine (17.3% vs. 7.0%, p = 0.016). No significant differences in inflammatory plasma biomarkers were observed between groups. CONCLUSIONS: Cyclosporine did not meet pre-specified efficacy thresholds for recovery or mortality in severe COVID-19 ARDS and was associated with a higher rate of serious adverse events. These results do not support its addition to standard care in this population.

An integrated One Health surveillance approach to Dirofilaria spp.: Linking mosquito xenomonitoring, blood-meal analysis and veterinary epidemiology.
Dirofilaria immitis and Dirofilaria repens are mosquito-borne filarioid nematodes of veterinary and public health importance whose distribution is expanding across Europe. This study developed an integrated One Health surveillance framework combining mosquito monitoring, molecular xenomonitoring, blood-meal analysis, and veterinary epidemiological data to assess Dirofilaria circulation and transmission dynamics. During the 2025 transmission season, mosquitoes were collected by the University of Parma in urban and peri-urban areas and by the Istituto Zooprofilattico Sperimentale della Lombardia ed Emilia-Romagna (IZSLER) in rural areas. Female mosquitoes were morphologically identified and analysed in pools by Real-time PCR for D. immitis and D. repens DNA. Positive pools were screened for West Nile virus, Usutu virus, and insect-specific flaviviruses in order to detect possible co-infection parasite-virus. Blood-fed mosquitoes were individually analysed by mitochondrial 12S and 16S rRNA sequencing to identify vertebrate hosts. Veterinary practices across Emilia-Romagna were surveyed for canine and feline dirofilariosis during 2024-2025. Overall, 11,225 females belonging to eight species were collected and 181 pools analysed. D. immitis predominated in urban collections, whereas D. repens was more frequent in peri-urban and rural areas. Aedes albopictus was the principal positive species in urban environments, while Aedes caspius predominated in rural settings. Humans were the predominant blood-meal host, followed by dogs, horses, cattle, and birds. Veterinary and vector surveillance showed poor agreement, indicating complementary epidemiological information. These findings highlight complex transmission patterns and support integrated One Health surveillance to improve risk assessment and guide evidence-based prevention and control strategies for Dirofilaria and other vector-borne zoonoses.

Determinants of orthoflavivirus tropism in humans: from cellular entry to organ-specific pathogenesis.
Orthoflaviviruses, including dengue virus, tick-borne encephalitis virus, West Nile virus, Zika virus, Japanese encephalitis virus, and yellow fever virus, cause a wide spectrum of diseases in humans despite sharing a similar genomic organization. These viruses pose a growing global threat as they are spreading widely, treatment options remain limited, and both climate change and expanding mosquito populations increase the risk of outbreaks worldwide. This review summarizes the determinants of their human tropism, the capacity to infect specific cell types, tissues, and organs. We synthesized current knowledge on how viral factors, including host factor utilization and immune cell trafficking, shape tropism across multiple layers. Central to this process are sequential host barriers that govern infection, including viral attachment, internalization, and replication. Understanding these determinants is essential for informing strategies to mitigate the global burden of these medically important pathogens.

Comparative analysis of central nervous system persistence of morbilliviruses across host species reveals shared features with subacute sclerosing panencephalitis.
BACKGROUND: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is a rare but always fatal neurological complication of measles, associated with persistent measles virus (MeV) infection of the central nervous system (CNS). MeV is detected in the brains of deceased SSPE patients as hypermutated viral genomes, which often contain premature stop codons in the matrix (M) gene and encode a hyperfusogenic fusion (F) protein. As a result, infected cells in the CNS cannot produce virions but rather transmit the viral ribonucleoprotein from cell-to-cell in a slow but progressive manner, which ultimately results in widespread MeV infection of the brain. However, our understanding of the pathogenesis of SSPE is constrained by the lack of animal models combined with a clinically silent incubation period of several years. MAIN TEXT: In a recent publication in PNAS, Daniel Roji et al. analysed animal morbillivirus sequences detected in the brains of persistently infected hosts, including a lynx (canine distemper virus, CDV), two seals (phocine distemper virus, PDV) and a dolphin (cetacean morbillivirus, CeMV). The authors describe that the morbillivirus sequences detected in these animals contained unique mutational signatures. The CDV, CeMV and one of the PDV sequences encoded nonfunctional M proteins and hyperfusogenic F proteins, reminiscent of the mutational profile of MeV detected in SSPE patients. Therefore, the authors conclude that human and animal morbilliviruses associated with chronic neurological infections share key genotypic and phenotypic traits, and that thorough analysis of naturally occurring animal morbillivirus infections could improve our understanding of SSPE pathogenesis. CONCLUSION: The comparison of neurological complications associated with human and animal morbillivirus infections as described by Daniel Roji et al. provides a unique One Health approach to understanding the drivers of SSPE. These findings may support the development of early diagnostics or an animal model for SSPE, providing an opportunity to test novel intervention strategies.

Fatal Occupational Leptospirosis in a Beef Cattle Farmer: Case Report and Epidemiological Investigation.
Leptospirosis is a re-emerging zoonosis responsible for approximately 1 million human infections and 59,000 deaths annually worldwide. In Europe, notification rates have increased by 5% per year since 2010, a trend compounded by climate change. The study was performed to document a fatal occupational case acquired through an under-recognised environmental exposure pathway, and to establish what regional surveillance data can and cannot support regarding its burden and exposure profile. We report a fatal case of occupational leptospirosis in a 56-year-old male beef cattle farmer in Lombardy (Po Valley, Italy) and describe the subsequent epidemiological investigation. Regional surveillance data, veterinary notifications, ECDC data, and an analysis of occupational and climate-related exposure pathways were reviewed. The index case was caused by a strain of serogroup Javanica (microscopic agglutination test titre 1:3,200 against serovar Poi), absent from standard regional animal serological screening panels, probably acquired through contaminated irrigation water. Among 16 confirmed leptospirosis cases in Lombardy over 22 months, 3 (18.8%) died and 1 (6.3%) had permanent disability (severe-outcome rate 25.0%, likely an underestimate given surveillance failures). Twelve of 16 cases (75.0%) had an agricultural-environmental exposure nexus. Leptospirosis risk in irrigated agriculture extends beyond livestock contact to environmental contamination of surface water by wildlife reservoirs. Climate change is expected to expand the disease's European distribution and extend the transmission season. A One Health approach integrating occupational medicine, veterinary surveillance, engineering controls, and climate-adaptive prevention is needed.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis suppresses protective Th17 responses during infection.
Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) causes more deaths annually than any other pathogen, yet an effective vaccine remains elusive. IFN-γ-producing Th1 CD4+ T cells are necessary but insufficient for protection against infection. In humans, the development of IL-17A-producing Th17 T cells correlates with protection; however, not all individuals develop a Th17 response. In mice, experimental vaccines can elicit protective Th17 cells, yet Th17s are rare in primary infection. Why Mtb fails to consistently elicit Th17s is unknown. Here, we identify factors suppressing Th17 responses during primary infection. We demonstrate that the lack of Th17 induction is independent of route and duration. Next, using Tbx21-deficient mice, we show that Mtb drives a Th1 response that is only partially protective and limits Th17 cell production in an IFN-γ-independent manner. We further reveal that the ESX-1 type VII secretion system and lipid phthiocerol dimycocerosate (PDIM) suppress Th17 responses. Infection with ESX-1 or PDIM mutants results in significantly increased Th17 T cells and IL-17A cytokine in the lungs, and infection of IL-17A-deficient animals partially restores virulence of ESX-1 and PDIM mutants. Although the ESX-1 secretion system and lipid PDIM elicit type I IFN, which can suppress Th17 differentiation, we find that suppression of Th17 is independent of type I IFN. Instead, ESX-1 and PDIM suppress production of IL-23, a cytokine that promotes Th17 differentiation, in dendritic cells found in mediastinal lymph nodes during Mtb infection. These findings define a new function of the ESX-1 secretion system and PDIM in Mtb virulence, a long-standing question in tuberculosis research.

Antibiotic Resistance in India Over a Decade: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Clinical and Molecular Evidence (2015-2025).
Antibiotic resistance is a major global public health threat that compromises the effectiveness of antibiotic agents and increases morbidity, mortality, and health care costs. India faces a substantial AMR burden driven by high infectious disease prevalence, widespread antibiotic use, and variable surveillance capacity. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to synthesize evidence on antibiotic resistance patterns in India from 2015 to 2025, estimate the prevalence of resistance among major bacterial pathogens, evaluate molecular resistance determinants, and assess mortality associated with resistant infections. A systematic search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, surveillance reports, and grey literature was conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Studies reporting antibiotic resistance data from India between January 2015 and December 2025 were included. Data extraction and quality assessment were performed independently by 2 reviewers. A random-effects meta-analysis was used to estimate the pooled prevalence of antibiotic resistance, molecular determinants of resistance, and mortality outcomes, and heterogeneity was assessed using the Cochrane Q and I2 statistics. Forty-six studies met the inclusion criteria. The pooled prevalence of antibiotic resistance was 55.7% (95% CI: 47.4%-63.9%; I2=98.6%). High resistance rates were reported among major gram-negative pathogens, particularly Klebsiella pneumoniae, Escherichia coli, Acinetobacter baumannii, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Molecular meta-analysis demonstrated a pooled prevalence of resistance-associated genes of 64.5% (95% CI: 46.0%-83.0%), with blaNDM, blaOXA-48-like, and blaKPC being the most frequently reported determinants. Mortality associated with resistant infections was 31.0% (95% CI: 18.2%-43.8%). Substantial heterogeneity was observed across all analyses. Available evidence indicates that antibiotic resistance remains a significant health care challenge in India. High levels of multidrug resistance, widespread dissemination of carbapenemase genes, and considerable mortality associated with resistant infections underscore the need for strengthened antibiotic stewardship, standardized surveillance, expanded molecular diagnostics, and coordinated public health interventions. However, the findings should be interpreted cautiously because of substantial heterogeneity and the predominance of studies from tertiary-care settings. This review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261406324).

Feasibility and clinical outcomes of routine point-of-care screening for opportunistic infections among people with advanced HIV disease in Guyana.
OBJECTIVES: We evaluated the feasibility and outcomes of implementing comprehensive Point-of-care (POC) opportunistic infections (OIs) screening among people with Advanced HIV disease (AHD) in Guyana. METHODS: We conducted a prospective multicentre cohort study across seven sites between February 2024 and March 2025. Adults with suspected AHD, defined as CD4 <200 cells/mm3 or signs/symptoms suggestive of OIs, were enrolled. All participants received a package for OI screening consisting of urinary TB-LAM, serum cryptococcal antigen, urinary Histoplasma antigen and rapid CD4 testing. Outcomes at 30 and 90 days were recorded. Primary outcome was feasibility, measured as the proportion completing the full screening panel. Secondary outcomes included diagnostic yield, care-package compliance and factors associated with negative outcomes (death or loss to follow-up). RESULTS: We enrolled 112 individuals; 88.4% completed the full diagnostic panel. A total of 24 participants had positive tests (21.4%). At 90 days, mortality was 5.4% and loss to follow-up was 11.6%. Positive diagnostic-test results were associated with worse outcomes at 30 and 90 days. In multivariable analysis, not initiating ART, requiring hospitalization for OI care or treatment, and lower haemoglobin independently predicted negative outcomes. Only 37.5% of participants with positive results completed the disease-specific diagnostic workup, and 41.7% initiated directed treatment for the detected OI. CONCLUSIONS: Routine POC screening for OIs among people with AHD in Guyana is feasible and detects a high burden of OIs. However, major gaps in completion of diagnostic algorithms, inconsistent availability of OI treatments and delays in ART initiation reduce the potential clinical impact of early detection.

The cell wall integrity pathway kinase Mpk1 regulates extracellular vesicle production and apoptotic-like vesicle release in Cryptococcus neoformans.
Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are important mediators of fungal physiology and host interactions, yet the mechanisms governing their production remain poorly understood. In Cryptococcus neoformans, EV production is tightly regulated by environmental conditions, suggesting the existence of dedicated signaling pathways. Here, we screened a kinase deletion library to identify regulators of EV production and found that the cell wall integrity (CWI) pathway acts as a major negative regulator of EV production. Deletion of the CWI kinases MPK1, MKK2, or BCK1 increased EV release. Unexpectedly, the size of EVs produced by CWI mutants differed markedly from wild type. Accordingly, cryo-electron microscopy revealed the accumulation of larger vesicles with altered size distributions in the mpk1Δ mutant. These EVs lacked the characteristic mannoprotein-based fibrillar surface decoration observed on most wild-type vesicles, exhibited reduced association with capsular polysaccharide, and contained substantially less protein. Quantitative proteomic analysis demonstrated extensive remodeling of the EV proteome, with depletion of glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored proteins, and enrichment of ribosomal proteins and histones. Finally, mpk1Δ EVs displayed several hallmarks of mammalian apoptotic EVs, including phosphatidylserine exposure, and were produced under conditions associated with reduced cell viability. Together, these findings identify the CWI pathway as a central regulator of fungal EV production and provide evidence that C. neoformans produces distinct EV populations through genetically regulated pathways. Our results provide evidence for an apoptotic-like EV population in fungi and reveal an unexpected link between cell wall integrity signaling, cell death, and EV diversity.IMPORTANCEFungal extracellular vesicles (EVs) contribute to virulence, antifungal resistance, and host-pathogen interactions, yet the mechanisms governing their production remain poorly understood. Here, we identify the cell wall integrity signaling pathway as a major regulator of EV production in the human fungal pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans. We further show that disruption of one of the major kinases of this pathway induces the production of a distinct population of EVs with structural and molecular features resembling mammalian apoptotic EVs. These findings demonstrate that fungi produce multiple EV populations through genetically regulated pathways rather than a single constitutive mechanism. By establishing the existence of apoptotic-like EVs in fungi, our work provides new insight into fungal EV production and lays the foundation for investigating how different EV populations contribute to fungal physiology, pathogenesis, and antifungal resistance.

Revealing the hidden burden: multiplex real-time PCR for 'endgame' surveillance of soil-transmitted helminthiasis in Fiji.
OBJECTIVES: Soil-transmitted helminthiasis (STH) remains a global health concern. As control programmes approach transmission interruption, sensitive diagnostics are needed to detect residual infections. This study compared conventional microscopy with real-time PCR for STH surveillance among primary schoolchildren in Fiji. METHODS: A total of 1,081 grade 1-2 children were screened by Kato-Katz (KK) thick smear and the formalin-ether concentration technique. A subset of samples was analysed by multiplex real-time PCR targeting Ascaris sp., Necator americanus, Ancylostoma sp., Trichuris trichiura, and Strongyloides sp.. RESULTS: In subgroup A (n = 90, a systematic 10% sample), real-time PCR detected any STH in 21.1% of children (19/90; 95% CI: 14.0-30.6) compared with 5.6% by microscopy (5/90; 95% CI: 2.4-12.4). Across all samples tested by real-time PCR (n = 133), hookworm was dominated by Necator americanus, exceeding Ancylostoma by ∼3:1. Ascaris cycle threshold values were strongly inversely correlated with KK egg counts (Spearman's ρ = -0.86, P < .001), confirming the semi-quantitative utility of real-time PCR. CONCLUSION: Multiplex real-time PCR reveals a greater STH burden than microscopy in this low-endemicity setting, providing species-level resolution and semi-quantitative capacity suitable for endgame surveillance. Quality-assured molecular diagnostics should be integrated into STH monitoring frameworks.

New abscisic acid analogues produced via genome mining-guided heterologous expression.
Abscisic acid (ABA), a pivotal phytohormone, was traditionally considered to be synthesized via the carotenoid pathway exclusively in plants. In our recent work, a dedicated ABA biosynthetic gene cluster (ablt) was discovered from the marine-derived fungus Alternaria alternata JJY-32 by genome mining. Heterologous expression of the ablt cluster in Aspergillus nidulans A1145 led to the production of two new analogues of ABA, designated as abaterpene A (1) and abaterpene B (2), along with six known sesquiterpenes. Further step-wise gene co-expression analysis demonstrated that ablt3 and ablt5 are necessary and sufficient for the production of compounds 1 and 2. The structures were determined using comprehensive 1D and 2D NMR data and assisted by ECD calculations.

Wavelength-Dependent Reduction of Newcastle Disease Virus Infectivity by Femtosecond Laser Irradiation: An In Ovo Proof-of-Concept Study.
Newcastle disease virus (NDV) causes substantial losses in poultry, and nonchemical approaches for reducing viral infectivity warrant investigation. Ultrafast femtosecond (fs) lasers offer a novel, non-thermal, and photosensitizer-free approach to pathogen inactivation. The primary aim of this study was to evaluate the wavelength-dependent efficacy of femtosecond laser irradiation (370-420 nm) in inactivating NDV, establishing a proof-of-concept for non-chemical viral attenuation using embryonated chicken eggs (ECEs) as a biological model. NDV suspensions were irradiated with 100 fs laser pulses at 370, 385, 400, and 420 nm for 60 min. The treated virus samples (100 µl) were inoculated into specific-pathogen-free (SPF) embryonated chicken eggs at dilutions of 10⁵, 10⁷ and 10⁹ and the viability of the embryo was monitored. Viral infectivity was assessed by embryo mortality and hemagglutination (HA) assays over 168 h. Exposure to 370 nm laser light resulted in > 99.99% reduction in viral infectivity and an estimated ≥ 4-log shift in the infectivity endpoint compared with the control, but complete inactivation was not observed. HA assays showed no protection at 385 and 400 nm on embryo death, but there was partial protection at 420 nm. Temperature monitoring did not show any thermal effects, indicating a non-thermal inactivation mechanism. This study demonstrates the strong antiviral potential of 370 nm femtosecond lasers against NDV; nevertheless, these findings justify further optimization of irradiation dose and independent confirmation by at least three serial passages. Viral antigen integrity, immunogenicity, and protective efficacy must be evaluated separately before any vaccine application.

Early Risk Stratification for Dengue Triage Using First-24-Hour Admission Data: A Multicentric Study.
BACKGROUND OBJECTIVES: Dengue outbreaks place substantial pressure on healthcare systems because many clinically stable patients are admitted for precautionary monitoring. Early triage remains challenging because mortality is rare and early clinical features often overlap between survivors and non-survivors. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective multicentric study of 1,148 laboratory-confirmed dengue patients, including 1,127 survivors and 21 non-survivors, admitted in India between 2012 and 2017. Only variables recorded within the first 24 hours of admission were analyzed. After nested cross-validated LASSO-based feature selection, ten machine learning classifiers were evaluated under three scenarios: default-threshold classification, SMOTE-based resampling, and cost-sensitive threshold optimization designed to reduce unsafe low-risk classification while preserving real-world outcome prevalence. RESULTS: Default-threshold models showed high overall accuracy but limited specificity for non-survivor identification. SMOTE improved minority-class recognition but altered classification behavior. Cost-sensitive threshold optimization improved balanced performance without changing the original class distribution. The threshold-optimized SVM model achieved specificity of 0.857, sensitivity of 0.914, balanced accuracy of 0.886, and correctly identified 18 of 21 non-survivors. Calibration analysis showed low Brier scores among top-performing models, and McNemar testing confirmed significant classification changes after threshold optimization for most classifiers. INTERPRETATION CONCLUSION: A survival-centric, cost-sensitive machine learning framework using first-24-hour admission data improved clinically relevant dengue triage performance while preserving real-world outcome prevalence. These findings support threshold-aware machine learning as a practical decision-support approach for risk-sensitive dengue triage during outbreak conditions.

Clinicodemographic and epidemiological factors associated with dengue severity and outcomes among hospitalized patients in Navi Mumbai, India: A retrospective study.
BACKGROUND OBJECTIVES: Dengue is a major public health concern in developing countries like India, with rising incidence in urban and peri-urban areas. Disease severity varies from mild illness to severe dengue with multiorgan dysfunction and mortality. To analyse clinicodemographic characteristics and predisposing risk factors associated with dengue severity and outcomes, and to assess duration of hospitalization across different severity categories. METHODS: A retrospective hospital-based study was conducted among 302 laboratory-confirmed dengue patients admitted to a tertiary care hospital in Navi Mumbai, Maharashtra, India, between July 2023 and December 2024. Dengue severity was classified as mild, moderate and severe as per National Guidelines for Clinical Management of Dengue Fever (2023). RESULTS: Majority were adults (75.2%) with male predominance (60.9%). Most cases were reported during the post-monsoon season. Moderate dengue constituted (64.9%) of cases, while (11.9%) being severe. Elderly age (OR = 4.35; 95% CI: 1.62-11.64) and presence of comorbidities (OR = 2.79; 95% CI: 1.25-6.24) were significantly associated with severe dengue (p < 0.05). Mean duration of hospitalization increased significantly with severity (mild: 4.0 days; moderate: 4.6 days; severe: 5.8 days; p < 0.001). Six deaths (2.0%) occurred among the 302 patients, all of which (16.7%) occurred in the severe dengue group. INTERPRETATION CONCLUSION: Elderly age and comorbidities were significantly associated with severe dengue. Investigations were classified according to whether a test and result were documented. Associations with outcome were assessed using Fisher's exact test and odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results Chest radiography was performed in 67/69 patients (97.1%). Five (38.5%) had a favorable outcome, and eight (61.5%) had an unfavorable outcome, including four subsequently diagnosed with malignant effusion and one death. Among 56 patients who underwent at least one pleural-fluid or tissue test, 39 (69.6%) had a favorable outcome. Primer: Orbiviruses.
Orbiviruses comprise numerous species and are transmitted by insect vectors. They are non-enveloped viruses with a multilayered capsid and a segmented double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) genome. Bluetongue virus (BTV), the prototype species of the genus Orbivirus, is a significant pathogen of livestock and is widely distributed throughout the world, causing serious periodic outbreaks with substantial economic consequences. Consequently, BTV has been extensively studied as a model orbivirus, resulting in a comprehensive understanding of its molecular epidemiology, genetics, biochemistry, structure, and replication cycle. This includes detailed insights into virus entry into host cells, synthesis of progeny viral components, assembly of new virions, and subsequent cell-to-cell transmission. This review summarizes the current literature on each of these aspects and discusses how this knowledge has been applied to develop novel vaccines against BTV and related orbiviruses. In addition, the review highlights important gaps in our understanding of virus replication within insect vectors, particularly Culicoides biting midges (gnats), at the molecular level. Addressing these gaps will provide valuable insights into orbivirus evolution, transmission, and the emergence of new viral strains.

Reliable early warning of infectious disease outbreaks remains a major challenge for surveillance systems, particularly for vector-borne pathogens whose transmission depends on interactions among hosts, vectors, and climate-sensitive environmental conditions. Data-driven forecasting offers a promising approach for predicting outbreak risk using surveillance and environmental data. This study develops a logit-weighted ensemble (LWE), a machine-learning framework that predicts outbreak occurrence 1-6 months ahead at the administrative unit-month scale using routinely available outbreak notifications and gridded climate data. Across all three countries, the LWE achieved the strongest and most stable predictive performance under a recall-focused evaluation that prioritises correctly identifying outbreak months. It outperformed or matched 14 benchmark models, with differences becoming more pronounced at longer lead times (month +3 onward), when predictions are more uncertain and outbreaks are relatively rare. Predictability varied across countries, with the highest performance in Greece, strong performance in France, and lower, more variable performance in Italy, reflecting differences in how consistently outbreaks occur and spread across regions. Overall, the results demonstrate that horizon-aware, climate-informed forecasting can reliably identify months and locations at elevated risk of outbreak occurrence up to six months in advance, supporting surveillance planning and preparedness across heterogeneous European settings. The ensemble framework provides a robust and portable strategy for outbreak prediction using routinely collected surveillance and environmental data.

A predictor-corrector product-integration scheme is then developed for the tempered system, and a mesh-refinement study confirms an empirical convergence order close to one. Ablation experiments show that the logarithmic state representation and the increment-based targets are the decisive design choices, while rollout fine-tuning further improves worst-case robustness of free-running predictions. The selected surrogate attains high one-step accuracy (RMSE 0.4121, MAE 0.1303, R2=0.999998) and, in fully free-running closed-loop mode, reproduces unseen tempered test scenarios with mean R2=0.9990 (mean RMSE 3.32) on the benchmark cases and R2=0.9973±0.0031 over a random evaluation suite of 18 unseen tempered scenarios; accuracy degrades only in the near-untempered long-memory limit λ → 0, which we characterize explicitly. Parameter-matched LSTM and GRU baselines trained under the identical protocol do not outperform the proposed feed-forward surrogate, and in batched operation the surrogate is about two orders of magnitude faster than the numerical solver.
